finding.claim: Missing authentication on the /settings/email state-changing endpoint: it uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. Its sibling /settings/password correctly uses @login_required.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37 (account email change, with uid None)

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid') and never aborts when absent
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called unconditionally, with g.uid possibly None
sibling /settings/password uses @login_required, which shows the intended control

finding.guards_checked: login_required (applied to password route only, not email route); no in-handler check of g.uid; no CSRF protection on either route. set_email is a stub (pass), so the impact depends on the real implementation. With uid None it could update a NULL/unscoped account row or silently fail. The missing auth guard on a sensitive account-modification route is the defect. Email change then allows account takeover through password reset.

verdict.guard_found: none on the email route; login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid and never aborts; no in-handler g.uid check; login_required (routes.py:8-16) exists but is applied only to the password route
verdict.reason: routes.py:34-38 exposes POST /settings/email with @login_optional (routes.py:22 sets g.uid=None, no abort), so an anonymous request calls set_email(None, ...) at line 37 with no check, unlike /settings/password's @login_required at line 42; impact is limited because set_email is a stub (line 48-49), but the missing auth guard is real.
